title: Bidirectional BFS in Salvador: Meet in the Middle
description: Watch Bidirectional BFS race through Salvador’s street grid by expanding search frontiers from both start and goal. The moment the two waves collide, the shortest path is reconstructed like a real-time map reveal.
ig_caption:
🌍🚦 **Bidirectional BFS in Salvador (Barra)**: faster shortest paths by splitting the search! 

Here’s the core idea from a graph-theory angle: treat the street map as an unweighted graph **G = (V, E)** where intersections are nodes (V) and streets are edges (E). Instead of running BFS from only the start, **Bidirectional BFS launches two BFS processes simultaneously**—one forward from the origin and one backward from the destination—each building layers of equal distance. When the frontiers intersect (a “meeting node”), we can combine the partial paths to reconstruct the shortest route. ⚡📍

Because both searches grow toward each other, this typically reduces explored nodes compared to single-source BFS on large graphs (especially when the shortest path is much smaller than the full search space). 🧠🔍

Try it on your next map: start and end anywhere in your city and watch the wavefronts converge! 👉🎥 Comment your favorite start/goal pins and **follow for more real-map algorithm visualizations**.

yt_description:
Explore **Bidirectional BFS** shortest path visualization in **Salvador (Barra)**! 🗺️⚡

In this YouTube Shorts, we convert real street maps into an **unweighted graph** and run **Bidirectional BFS** by expanding two BFS wavefronts from start and goal until they intersect. This “meet in the middle” approach reduces explored nodes and reconstructs the shortest path immediately when frontiers collide.
